thread.title: It's Time To Put Up Or Sell Off

author: Eric Parnell, CFA
title: It's Time To Put Up Or Sell Off
text:
"Put up or shut up, we're not wasting time again,The credits are rolling and we're getting lost again"
- Break Out! Break Out!, All Time Low, 2006
It all comes down to this It has been more than six months since the major U.S. tax cuts passed through Washington. As it was told at the start of the year, lower corporate tax rates were to bring with them an increase in economic activity and fixed investment that would result in more robust and sustainable growth going forward. After waiting more than half a year, we will find out much more definitively in the next three weeks whether all of the money being stuffed into corporate coffers ends up being worth it for the U.S. economy and its markets. If not, investors might start hearing the ringing of bells for the bull market in the distance.
Mr. Keynes rolls over in his grave Both the fiscal policy timing and implementation of the tax cut legislation was dubious from a Keynesian economics perspective to say the least for the following reasons.
Timing The major tax cuts came not during recession but instead during the eighth year of one of the longest economic expansions in history.
Deficit The major tax cuts did not identify inefficiencies that could result in a lowering of the deficit and the debt, much less a deficit neutral solution. Instead, it is expected that the tax plan will increase the debt by $1.5 trillion. This estimate, of course, will likely end up being more in reality when it's all said and done.
Incentives The major tax cuts did not include incentives encouraging companies to deploy their windfall in productive capital spending initiatives in support of the sustainable health of the broader economy. Instead, it is estimated that more than $800 billion and as much as $1 trillion or more could end up heading back out the doors of corporations in the form of largely unproductive dividends and share repurchases once 2018 draws to a close. This total would easily exceed the previous all-time annual record set in - wait for it - 2007. Dubious indeed!
Put simply, this tax cut is coming at a huge cost. The fiscal policy treasure that might have been available for deployment during the next recession is now gone. It sure as heck better be worth it. And we will begin to truly find out in a big way over the next four weeks between now and August 3.
2018 Q2 earnings season starts Tuesday Before the market opens on Tuesday, PepsiCo (NYSE: PEP ) will step to the podium and kick off the latest quarterly earnings season. The major banks of Citigroup (NYSE: C ), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM ) and Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC ) follow on Friday. And over the next three weeks that follow, nearly 400 companies in the S&P 500 Index will report their latest quarterly results. More importantly, many of these same companies will be issuing forward guidance on what investors should expect in terms of revenues, earnings, and business activity for the coming quarters.
Why does this reporting season matter so much? The tax cuts came just as the calendar was flipping to 2018. As a result, most corporations spent much of the first quarter simply working to understand and adjust to the new tax laws. Thus, by the end of the first quarter, they likely would have had little time if any to consider new capital budgeting projects to implement with their newly found tax cut treasure. But coming out of the second quarter, companies likely have a much better idea of how they intend on deploying this additional capital on capital expenditures and fixed investment so that the benefit that is showing up for companies on an after-tax basis can start to feed through to pick up earnings on a before tax basis, which is where the higher multiplier effect will start to kick in for the broader economy.
Personally, I am looking forward to learning more about what companies intend to do. Unfortunately, as evidenced by Apple's (NASDAQ: AAPL ) announcement in May that they intend to buyback an extraordinary $100 billion in stock plus on top of adding another $3 billion per year in dividend payments on top of the more than $12 billion per year already being paid out, I think I already know the answer.
Expectations are already high An additional challenge face companies as they head into 2018 Q2 earnings season. What if it turns out that they can't deliver on the elements to boost economic growth even if they wanted to? Corporate earnings expectations are already high and have been for some time. In other words, the anticipated strength of corporate earnings in the coming quarters should already be priced into the market.
Companies have been scaling back expectations since May At the end of April, S&P 500 Index earnings had been revised higher since the start of the year by more than +2% for 2018 Q2, +6% for 2018 Q3 and nearly +14% for 2018 Q4. But over the past two months since, corporations have been slowly walking back earnings forecasts. And following the -2% to -3% cut in quarterly earnings forecasts for each of the next three quarters (2018 Q2, Q3, and Q4) in just the past week ahead of the start of earnings season, we may only be getting started in companies working to guide forward earnings expectations back to earth.
Q2 earnings are already below where the forecasts from the start of the year when the tax cuts were first announced, while Q3 is now only +1% higher and Q4 only +7% greater with potentially six more months of downward revisions ahead. One can only hope that major corporate tax cuts do not end up leading to earnings that end up being lower than the expectations that existed before the tax cuts were even a done deal at the end of 2017.
What if companies fall short? The negative impact of the tax cuts falling short of high expectations cannot be overstated. The S&P 500 Index is already trading at 24 times trailing 12-month as reported earnings at the present time, which ranks among the highest market valuations in history. Historically, stocks have registered an annualized return over the subsequent ten years of worse than -1%. Put more directly, whenever stocks have been priced this high in the past, they have generated a negative nominal return for investors over the next decade. And stocks have been this expensive if not more so for a few years now.
So, if stocks want to keep their legendary bull market streak going, companies need to deliver on earnings expectations and then some. For even if they hit currently high expectations over the next three quarters and the S&P 500 Index does nothing more than stay flat, they will still be trading at 19 times earnings, which is a +20% premium over the historical average from which ten-year annualized returns are still negative, just less so. Thus, if it turns out that stocks end up falling short of current expectations with a steady stream of downward revisions between now and when companies are reporting during the 2018 Q4 earnings season in January, it will make the outlook for U.S. stocks going forward all the more challenging.
Then, there's the margin compression threat Corporate profit margins are riding at an all-time high on an operating earnings basis - they have been notably falling on a tax reporting basis since 2012 - but how long can this be expected to last with the year-over-year change in the producer price index (PPI) currently well over +5% running well in excess of the consumer price index (CPI) at less than +3%, a spread that has been in place for more than a year and counting? And with wages also reportedly on the rise at the same time that the breakeven inflation rate remains stubbornly at +2%, such are the forces of margin compression and subsequently lower valuation multiples and stock prices.
And none of this factors in the potential spillover effects from the ongoing trade conflict, the sharply strengthening U.S. dollar for the past three months and counting, rising borrowing costs, thanks to the U.S. Federal Reserve that is planning potentially two more rate hikes in 2018 and even more next year, or the fact that central bank stimulus is now flowing out of the global economy, in aggregate on net, for the first time in the post crisis period.
It is time for companies to put up... It all comes down to this. Roughly 400 companies in the S&P 500 index will be reporting earnings between now and August 3. Many of these companies will be updating their forward guidance for the rest of 2018 and beyond. The U.S. stock market has already had a choppy year so far, but its spirits have been kept up in large part by the high hopes for corporate earnings. And for these corporate earnings to continue to grow in any sustainable way going forward, companies need to show that they are spending money on growth driving capital expenditures and fixed investment initiatives. For the gravy train of easy money and low interest rates is quickly going away. And the sugar high of corporate tax cuts will only last so long before that too has run its course.
... Or sell off If companies are unable to deliver on high earnings expectations, while also meeting lofty forward guidance expectations, we may finally find ourselves at the time where the stock market starts selling off in earnest. Stocks have held support admirably since the initial sell off in January, although key technical levels are increasingly coming into view. If companies start falling short of expectations and/or lowering forward guidance, and if stocks respond accordingly, key levels to watch on the S&P 500 Index include the 50-day moving average currently at 2,726 and rising, the 200-day moving average at 2,675 and rising, and the 400-day moving average at 2,527 and rising. Each of these levels should easy be considered to be in play on any market sell-off in the coming weeks. And if the 400-day moving average were to be broken in the process, it would be time to engage a new discussion about the sustainability of the bull market going forward.
What to do? It may very well turn out that companies exceed expectations and remain as optimistic as ever about the outlook. We will know a lot more in the next few weeks. But what can investors reasonably do on the portfolio margins to prepare for a more disappointing earnings season outcome if they are not positioned already? This will be the topic of an upcoming Instablog post on Seeking Alpha in the coming days.
